content_voiceover: This diagram lays out the vitamin K cycle that warfarin disrupts. Gamma-glutamyl carboxylase uses reduced vitamin K to carboxylate glutamate residues on the inactive precursors of clotting factors two, seven, nine, and ten, converting them into their active, calcium-binding forms. That reaction oxidizes vitamin K in the process, and the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, or VKOR, normally regenerates reduced vitamin K from its oxidized form so the cycle can continue. Warfarin works by inhibiting VKOR, shown here crossed out, which depletes the pool of reduced vitamin K and therefore prevents carboxylation and activation of factors two, seven, nine, and ten, along with proteins C and S. Because this is an enzyme inhibition mechanism rather than a direct anticoagulant effect, warfarin's clinical effect is delayed until existing active clotting factors clear from circulation. The slide also lists the major variables that affect an individual's warfarin dose requirement and response: genetic polymorphisms in CYP2C9, which metabolizes warfarin, and in VKOR itself, along with dietary vitamin K intake, which can antagonize or potentiate the drug's effect depending on consistency of intake.
keypoints: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR)
This blocks regeneration of reduced vitamin K needed for carboxylation
Affects factors II, VII, IX, X plus proteins C and S
Warfarin response varies with CYP2C9 genotype, VKOR polymorphism, and dietary vitamin K
keypoint_voiceover: Warfarin blocks VKOR, cutting off the supply of reduced vitamin K needed to activate factors two, seven, nine, and ten, plus proteins C and S. Dosing varies with CYP2C9 and VKOR genetics and with dietary vitamin K intake.
